title: The Three Questions Every Magic System Needs

voice.direction: A calm, practical guide with a hint of delight. The hook is an invitation, not a warning. Each question ('One', 'Two', 'Three') gets a short beat before its answer, said plainly like filling in a form. 'Then the queen's crown shatters' drops low; 'A thief.' lands with a small smile. 'Can. Can't. Costs.' is three even taps. The save CTA is friendly. No trailer voice.

lines.text: Before inventing a spell, answer these three questions.
One: what can it do? Menders fix anything broken.
Two: what stops it? Only what they touched before it broke.
Three: what does it cost? Each mend cracks something they own.
The only mender who ever held it? A thief.
Three answers, and the story writes itself.
Can. Can't. Costs. Answer all three before your first spell.
Save this before designing your next magic system.

lesson: Before inventing a spell, answer three questions: what can the magic do (capabilities), what stops it from doing everything (limitations), and what does using it cost (consequences). Together the three answers immediately generate story: menders fix anything broken, but only what they touched before it broke, and each mend cracks something they own, so when the queen's crown shatters and the only mender who ever held it is a thief, the plot is already there.

youtube.description:
Before inventing a spell, answer these three questions.

One: what can it do? Menders fix anything broken. Two: what stops it? Only what they touched before it broke. Three: what does it cost? Each mend cracks something they own.

Then the queen's crown shatters, and the only mender who ever held it is a thief. Why did a thief hold the crown? Will she mend it? What will crack in her own home? Three answers, and the story writes itself.

Capabilities, limitations, consequences: can, can't, costs. Answer all three before your first spell, and your magic starts making plot instead of solving it.

Save this before designing your next magic system.
